issues: Whether the officer's finding that the marriage is not genuine and was entered primarily for immigration purposes under s.4(1) of the IRPR was reasonable

Whether an officer may consider a sponsor's prior marriages, divorces and previous sponsorship history (including a prior refusal on marriage-of-convenience grounds) in assessing genuineness of a subsequent marriage

Whether reliance on demeanour, body language and an adversarial interview approach ('answer truthfully' warning) renders the decision procedurally unfair or gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias

Whether discrepancies between spouses on collateral details (region of origin, timeline of meeting/cohabitation, honeymoon/vacation destinations, work schedule) can reasonably support a marriage-of-convenience finding
Whether the birth of a child during the relationship is determinative of, or must be given significant weight in assessing, genuineness of the marriage
Whether the officer adequately engaged with the evidence and provided sufficient reasons to meet the reasonableness standard under Vavilov
What weight, if any, should be given to the fact that cohabitation began before the sponsor's divorce from his previous wife was finalized
key_facts: Client is a woman in her thirties from South Asia, initially in Canada on a temporary work permit
Sponsor is a Canadian citizen roughly twenty years older, himself sponsored to Canada decades ago via spousal sponsorship
Sponsor has since married and filed sponsorship/spousal applications for four other women from the same country, one refused on marriage-of-convenience grounds
Client began cohabiting with sponsor while he was still legally married to a previous wife; he divorced her and married the client a few weeks later
Couple now has a baby daughter together

At an in-person interview, officer questioned them separately then together and found inconsistencies: neither knew the other's region of origin, differing accounts of when they met, when cohabitation began, honeymoon and last vacation destinations, and client did not know husband's work schedule
Officer refused the application relying heavily on sponsor's marital/sponsorship history and on the couple's demeanour and body language
Clients allege the officer had prejudged the outcome and treated them adversarially, including a warning to answer truthfully before the interview began
causes_of_action: Application for judicial review of a visa/immigration officer's refusal decision
Refusal of spousal sponsorship application under s.4(1) IRPR (marriage not genuine / entered primarily to acquire status)
candidate_statutes: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27
Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227, s. 4(1)
Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7 (judicial review provisions)
